What this report is: the result of Project 10’s brand archetype assessment, scored with Skyway’s weighted 37-point engine across all twelve archetypes, then translated into identity, voice, competitive position and visual direction. Every score in it is a real number from your own answers, and every answer you gave is printed in the second tab.
01 · Brand Identity

You don’t teach the student. You teach everyone standing around them.

Two archetypes came back two points apart, which the engine calls a dual read. Sage at 10 and Creator at 8 are not a leader and a footnote. They are two halves of one job: you find out what a student with a disability actually needs to reach adulthood in Florida, and then you build the thing that gets it into an educator’s hands.

Sage · 10 · Understanding
Knowing what comes next

A statewide network whose real product is knowledge: what the law requires, what the evidence supports, and what actually happens to a student the year after the diploma.

  • “Wise and knowledgeable” is the character you chose for the brand, word for word.
  • You picked the Owl as your ambassador and the candle flame as your symbol. Both belong to the Sage.
  • Among your three fears sits misinformation — the Sage’s fear, verbatim.
Creator · 8 · Innovation
Building what isn’t there yet

The knowing never stays abstract. It becomes a module, a toolkit, a template a district can open on a Monday and use before lunch.

  • Your motto: “If it can be imagined, it can be created.” That is the Creator’s line, not a paraphrase of it.
  • Two of your three strengths are transformative and innovative.
  • You asked for custom iconography and a mark built on a person growing into a tree. You think in things you make.

At the core, you’re a Sage.

The Sage’s drive is understanding, and the Sage’s promise is that understanding changes what a person can do. Your answers say it three separate ways: the owl, the candle flame, and “wise and knowledgeable” as the brand’s character. In this business that has a very specific meaning. A teacher does not come to you because she lacks goodwill. She comes because nobody has ever told her, plainly, what a transition IEP has to contain by the student’s sixteenth birthday, or who to call at Vocational Rehabilitation, or what the last five years of data say about work-based learning. You are the answer to that. Lean into: the answer before the offer, plain language over compliance language, and teaching an educator something she can use without you next time.

Creator is the other half, not the delivery.

Two points is a narrow margin and the honest reading is a pairing. Where a pure Sage would publish, you build. Your motto is the Creator’s, your strengths are the Creator’s, and the logo you imagined is a Creator’s brief: a person growing into a tree, drawn from scratch, with custom iconography. This is the half that keeps the Sage from becoming a library. Understanding that arrives as a PDF of regulations is not understanding; understanding that arrives as a one-page planning tool with your name on it is. Lean into: named, dated, downloadable things — and the confidence to invent the tool that does not exist yet rather than pointing at somebody else’s.

Why the combination is one-of-a-kind.

The twelve archetypes group into four families by underlying drive, and your points land almost exactly across two of them: Spiritual carries 15 of 37, Structural carries 14. One point apart. Sage sits in Spiritual; Creator sits in Structural. Most brands have a centre of gravity in one family, which makes them legible and slightly predictable. Yours genuinely straddles two, and the crossing is the whole identity: a knowing organisation that builds, or a building organisation that knows first. The two low families are just as informative — Legacy at 5 and Connector at 3. You are not a movement, and you are not a community. You are a resource, and you would rather be right than beloved.

The one thing to make unmistakable
Every organisation in this category offers training and technical assistance. Almost none of them hand you the finished thing and say: here, use this on Monday.
“If it can be imagined, it can be created.”
Your own motto · the Creator’s line, verbatim · and the second-highest score in the read
One number is worth sitting with: Caregiver 2. A disability-services network scored 2 out of 37 on Service. That is not a gap and it is not a warning. It is the sharpest thing in the read: you do not see yourselves as caring for students. You see yourselves as equipping the adults who do. Your own differentiator says so — you support the educators who improve outcomes. Hold that. The whole category talks about students; almost nobody talks to the person holding the caseload.

The guardrail: Sage leads, Creator builds. Teach before you help, and never let the building outrun the knowing. If a resource ships without a reason attached, it’s the wrong resource. If a reason ships without a resource attached, it’s only half your brand.

Sage · in your words

Three separate answers land on the same archetype. Your brand’s character is “wise and knowledgeable.” Your symbol is a candle flame. Your ambassador is the owl. And one of your three fears is misinformation, which is the Sage’s fear stated exactly. Understanding is the product.

Creator · in your words

Your motto is “if it can be imagined, it can be created” and two of your three strengths are transformative and innovative. The brief you wrote for the mark — a person growing into a tree, with custom iconography — is a Creator’s brief. You do not point at resources. You make them.

Ruler · the real third

At 4, Ruler is the only archetype with any distance on the pack. Your stated purpose was “to provide structure for others” and your problem approach was “strategic vision.” That is the state-network half of the brand: frameworks, sequence, a defensible order of operations. It belongs in the posture, not in the voice.

The zeros, which are findings

Everyman 0. You chose the community center as your setting and belonging still scored nothing — you gather people, but you are not one of the crowd, you are the one with the answer. Jester 0, against “Playful / Whimsical” as your first style word. Outlaw 0: you improve the system from inside it, which for a network housed at a state university is the correct answer.

Creator · 8InnovationThe other half. Your motto verbatim, plus “transformative” and “innovative.” → Named tools, custom iconography, things that did not exist before you built them.

Explorer · 3FreedomThe travel guide you chose as your character. Someone who has walked the route and will walk it with you. A useful metaphor for the brand, not a driver.

The centre of gravity: Spiritual carries 15 of 37 and Structural carries 14 — one point apart, with Legacy at 5 and Connector at 3 far behind. Read that aloud and it is the whole brand: knowing and building, almost exactly balanced, and very little else competing for the room.

03 · Core Purpose

Make the last year of school the first year of a life.

Project 10 exists so that the adults around a student with a disability — the teacher, the transition specialist, the district administrator, the parent at the table — know exactly what comes next and have the tool in front of them to do it. You do not hand the student the future. You hand the people responsible for the student what that future requires, early enough for it to matter.

It is the Sage’s purpose — understanding is what changes the outcome — delivered the Creator’s way: as something built, named and usable, rather than something published and hoped for.

Alternates to react to

Every student leaves school. We make sure somebody planned for what happens next.

We don’t serve students. We serve the people who do — which is how you reach thousands of them.

Cultivators of growth, connections and possibilities. Growth takes a gardener, and the gardener needs tools.

04 · Voice & Personality

Speak like the colleague who already found the answer.

If the brand were a person: a veteran transition specialist who has sat in IEP meetings in half the districts in Florida, keeps a folder of the forms that actually work, answers email on a Friday afternoon, and has never once made a teacher feel behind for asking. She knows the statute and she will not quote it at you. She has an opinion about which order to do things in, and she will tell you why.

Knowledgeable

We are current, evidence-backed, plain  ·  not academic, acronym-drunk, or compliance-flavoured.
“Here’s what the research says, and here’s the form you’ll actually need on Monday.”

Resourceful

We are inventive, practical, willing to build the thing that doesn’t exist  ·  not gimmicky, novel for its own sake, or another pilot.
“There wasn’t a tool for this, so we made one. It’s two pages.”

Approachable

We are warm, unhurried, jargon-free  ·  not chummy, cutesy, or quietly condescending.
“There’s no question here you should already know the answer to. Ask us that one.”

Guiding

We are clear about the next step, honest about the hard ones  ·  not vague, cheerleading, or evasive about what the system can’t do.
“This part is genuinely difficult. Here’s the order we’d do it in.”

On the dials: guide over authority · plain over technical · practical over theoretical · specific over comprehensive · warm over formal · and always the answer before the offer.

Training session blurb

“Ninety minutes on writing transition goals a student can actually name. You’ll leave with the template and three examples from Florida districts.”

Email to a district

“You asked what changes for your juniors this year. Short answer below, and the one-pager is attached — forward it to your case managers as is.”

Trade show line

“Tell us the part of transition planning your teachers dread most. We’ve almost certainly built something for it.”

The guardrail: you chose “Playful / Whimsical” as a style word and Jester scored zero. Both are true, and they belong in different places. The play lives in the iconography and the illustration — leaves, growth marks, a mark that rewards a second look. It does not live in the copy. A sentence that is trying to be charming is a sentence an overloaded teacher has to read twice.
Part II · The Strategy

Now that we know who you are, here’s how you win.

The identity only matters if it opens a lane nobody else can follow you into. So we mapped the field an educator is actually choosing between when she needs help with transition planning in Florida — and it sorts into three camps, none of which is standing where you are.

05 · Competitive Landscape

Three camps. None of them own your lane.

You left the rivals question open, so we scoped this to the market reach you gave us: statewide Florida, educators and districts serving students with disabilities. The honest framing is that you rarely lose a sale — you lose an educator’s attention. When a teacher needs help with transition planning, three kinds of organisation are competing for the hour she has. (Read from each organisation’s public positioning as of 31 August 2026, and to be validated with you on the review call — particularly the first camp, where you know the internal reality far better than any public page shows it.)

Camp One
The sibling state projects
WhoFDLRS, the Florida Inclusion Network, SEDNET, FLPBIS:MTSS, CARD — the other BEESS discretionary projects, most of them housed at universities like you Our readCaregiver + Ruler. Service delivered inside a system, framed by compliance and coverage VoiceAcronym-first and institutional; “training and technical assistance,” “regional facilitators,” “deliverables” You winThey are each named for a function. You can be named for an outcome — growth, connections, possibilities — which is the only brand in the family a teacher could describe to a colleague without a glossary.
Camp Two
The national transition authorities
WhoNTACT:C, PACER’s transition and employment resources, Think College, the Zarrow Institute, CEC’s Division on Career Development and Transition Our readSage + Ruler. Research-to-practice, evidence-based predictors, national frameworks VoiceScholarly and federal; “evidence-based practices,” “capacity building,” citations everywhere You winThey write for fifty states. You know which Florida district, which form, and who to call there. National authority is not the same thing as being reachable on a Tuesday.
Camp Three
The curriculum and platform vendors
WhoAttainment Company, n2y and Unique Learning System, transition-curriculum publishers, and the paid conference PD circuit Our readCreator + Ruler. Product thinking, licensing tiers, adoption cycles VoiceCommercial and confident; “solutions,” “engagement,” “research-based,” a demo request on every page You winThey ship a product a district buys once. You are free, statewide, and still there after the purchase order closes. Nobody else can be both the vendor and the neighbour.
The open lane
One organisation that is all three at once: Florida-specific, genuinely expert, and shipping finished tools.

The sibling projects are organised around functions, the national centres are organised around research, and the vendors are organised around a sale. Your two highest scores are the two halves nobody else holds together: the Sage who knows what actually works, and the Creator who has already built the thing that puts it to work. That is the lane. It is currently unoccupied, and it is describable in one sentence, which is rarer.

06 · Differentiation Strategy

Five ways to pull away

Each pillar targets the open lane, and each is something the brand should actively say out loud, not merely imply.

Lead with the tree, not the acronym.

You already made this call — no “Transition Education Network” in the mark — and it is the single most strategic instruction in your brief. Your entire field speaks in initials: FDLRS, FIN, SEDNET, BEESS, NTACT:C. An educator has to be taught what every one of them means before she can want anything from them. A plain-English name attached to a picture of growth is legible on sight, which in this category is close to a category of one.

In the brandThe mark is “Project 10” plus the cultivator line, and nothing else. The legal name lives in the footer, the grant citation and the compliance documents — never in the logo lockup, the booth header or the slide template.

Ship the built thing, not the technical assistance.

“Training and technical assistance” is the phrase every organisation in camps one and two uses, in those exact six words. It is not that the others do it badly; it is that the buyer cannot referee the claim. She has no way to tell one offer of technical assistance from the next, so she picks whoever she has heard of. What she can referee is a named tool she can open. Creator at 8 says this is already how you work — the strategic move is to make it the thing you are known for rather than a by-product of the grant.

In the brandGive every resource a name, a version and a date, the way software ships. Lead the site and the booth with the tools, not the services. Retire “training and technical assistance” from anything a teacher reads.

Be the one who knows Florida.

The national centres publish for every state, which means they have to stay one level above the specifics that actually block a transition IEP. That generality is a structural constraint, not a shortcoming — and it is exactly the gap you can fill without arguing with anyone. You know which Florida form, which agency, which regional contact, which deadline in this school year. Say “in Florida” in the copy relentlessly; it is a claim only you and your sibling projects can make, and only you are also shipping the tool.

In the brandEvery resource carries a Florida framing in its first line. Where a national practice needs translating into Florida procedure, publish the translation — that document is the most defensible thing you own.

Talk to the adult, on purpose.

Caregiver came back at 2 out of 37, and that is the read telling you something true: your customer is not the student. The entire category writes about students — outcomes, pathways, populations — and addresses the professional as an afterthought. Address her directly instead. She is carrying a caseload, a compliance calendar and forty families, and nobody is speaking to her as the person who has to make it happen by Friday.

In the brandWrite in the second person to the educator, not the third person about students. “You’ll need this before the March IEP” beats “students benefit from early planning” every time.

Show growth over time, because that is the word you chose.

“Cultivators” is a promise about duration, and the category reports in outputs: sessions delivered, attendees trained, districts reached. Nobody shows the arc. A student’s transition is a five-year story and you are one of the few organisations positioned to tell it across those years, in the same format, annually. That is a Sage’s evidence and a Creator’s artefact at once.

In the brandPublish one longitudinal piece a year in a fixed format — the same student cohort, the same measures, the same design. It compounds into the thing nobody can copy, because they would have to have started five years ago.

Your strategic sweet spot
The Florida network that knows, and builds.

Statewide expertise in transition, delivered as finished tools an educator can use the same week — addressed to her, in plain English, under a name she can repeat.

07 · Visual Identity · Concept Strategies

Three ways to look the part

Direction, not decoration: three strategic concepts, each true to Sage × Creator and each buildable across the surfaces you named — website, print, signage, apparel and the trade show floor. The designed colour boards come next; this section is the thinking they will be built from.

Concept A
The cultivated grid

Modern, geometric, unmistakably built.

A disciplined system with a visible structure: a clear grid, geometric shapes, generous space, and colour used in flat confident fields. The Creator half, expressed as craft rather than whimsy. It looks like something that was designed on purpose by people who make things.

Pros
  • Reads modern and current next to the sibling projects, which mostly do not
  • Scales cleanly from a 3 m trade show banner to a favicon
  • Cheapest to maintain across a small team and many templates
Tradeoffs
  • Risks feeling cool and institutional without warm photography
  • Geometric is the default of every ed-tech brand; it needs one strange, ownable move to escape
Concept B
Growth marks

The mark is a system, not a logo.

Your person-growing-into-a-tree idea, developed as a family: one primary mark plus a set of custom icons drawn from the same growth language — a shoot, a branch, a root, a canopy — each one standing for a stage of transition or a resource type. The “10” is drawn, not typed, and becomes the ownable glyph.

Pros
  • Delivers the custom iconography in your scope as strategy, not ornament
  • Gives every resource a visual label, which makes the toolkit navigable
  • The only concept here that no other BEESS project could plausibly adopt
Tradeoffs
  • Most design investment up front, and it needs governance to stay coherent
  • Growth-and-tree imagery is common in education; the drawing has to be genuinely distinctive
Concept C
The field guide

Sage first. The trusted reference.

An editorial system built for reading: strong typographic hierarchy, restrained colour, real photography of Florida classrooms and worksites, and layouts that make a dense document feel navigable. It looks like the book on the shelf everyone borrows and nobody returns.

Pros
  • Best of the three at the thing you actually do most — long documents
  • Carries authority with FDOE and district leadership on sight
  • Ages slowly and survives a change of design hands
Tradeoffs
  • Underplays the Creator half, your second-highest score
  • Furthest from the “playful” and “artistic” style words you chose
  • Depends on a real photo library, and consented photography of students is slow to build

The color thinking

You already have the palette and no logo to preserve, which is the easiest brief in branding: a colour system with nothing to unpick. It also agrees with the archetypes, which is not always the case. Sand #EDEBD1 and seaglass #80B0A6 read cultivated rather than clinical, and lemongrass #DBE442 is the colour of new growth — literally the first leaf. “Cultivators” and these three colours are the same idea. Two things need naming before it goes to design, and neither is an aesthetic objection.

Contrast, first, because of who you serve. A brand for the disability community gets judged on legibility before it is judged on taste, and as the palette stands there is no ink in it. Seaglass on sand measures 2.01:1 against the 4.5:1 that body text requires. Lemongrass on sand is 1.15:1, which is effectively invisible. There is no pairing of your three colours that can legally set a paragraph. The fix is one addition rather than a rethink: a deepened seaglass at roughly #2E5A52 stays unmistakably the same colour, clears 6.45:1 on sand, and becomes the working ink for type, rules and the mark. Take it further to #24413C — 9.18:1 — for dark surfaces like the trade show wall and the reversed lockup. Your two light colours then do the job they are genuinely good at: backgrounds with dark text over them, where seaglass reads at 7.05:1 and lemongrass at 12.34:1.

Two collisions to steer around. Seaglass over sand is the Florida coastal palette — every beach rental, resort and Gulf-side realtor in the state uses some version of it. On statewide signage and on apparel at a trade show it will read vacation before it reads education. The deepened seaglass solves most of that by itself, because the coastal version of this palette is always pale. Second, you are housed at USF: when that darker green goes in, keep it cool and blue-leaning rather than letting it drift toward a true green, or next to a USF booth the mark reads as a university sub-brand instead of a statewide network. #2E5A52 sits on the right side of that line; anything warmer does not.

Lemongrass is the ownable one, and it needs a ceiling. It is the single colour in the set no beach brand would use, which makes it your recognisable note rather than a garnish. Cap it at about five percent — a background block, an icon fill, an active state — and never a large field. At scale that yellow-green reads as hi-vis safety, and on a page in a school it reads as a highlighter.

And one conflict worth keeping. “Playful / Whimsical” was your first style word; Jester scored zero. Both are honest. Put the play in the drawing — the icons, the growth marks, the illustration — and keep the palette and the copy composed. Whimsy in the pictures reads as care; whimsy in the colour reads as a children’s programme, and your audience is professional adults.

The type thinking

You asked for geometric and modern, and the Sage×Creator pairing wants exactly that with one caveat: the default geometric is the single most-used voice in education marketing. Poppins and its neighbours are on half the district PD decks in the state. Choosing one makes you legible and invisible at the same moment.

The recommendation is a geometric skeleton with real character for display — Archivo or Instrument Sans both hold a headline and stay serious — over a workhorse chosen for long-form reading rather than for looks. Mulish or Nunito Sans have the open apertures and tall x-height that keep a dense resource readable at 14px in a PDF a teacher opens on her phone. That is not a small consideration for you; it is most of what your audience does with your work. If the “artistic / creative” note needs somewhere to live, Fraunces in a single warm display moment will carry it without touching the body text.

Mixed case, as you preferred, and we’d push it further. Your entire field sets its names in all-caps initials. Mixed case is not just a preference here, it is a differentiator you get for free. And the 10 is the most ownable glyph you have — a numeral in a category of acronyms. Draw it rather than setting it, and let it be the thing the tree grows through.

Our lean: Concept B, built with Concept A’s discipline. The growth-mark system delivers the custom iconography you scoped and the person-into-a-tree idea you already have, while the grid keeps it from drifting into decoration — and it is the only one of the three that a sibling project could not adopt next year.
08 · Summary

A Sage that builds. A Creator that knows why.

Sage 10, Creator 8, two points apart and one point separating the two families they come from. In a category split between projects named after their functions, national centres writing for fifty states, and vendors selling a licence, the open lane belongs to the organisation that knows what actually works in Florida and has already built the thing that puts it to work. Cultivators of growth, connections and possibilities — which is the name you gave yourselves before you took the assessment.

Slate & Seaglass

Selected

The selected system. A cool slate carries the working weight so Seaglass and Lemongrass are the only color in the system — white and the slate neutrals do the structure; the client's colors do the personality. Composed enough for district and state-level documents, warm enough for family-facing pages.

Gradient · Slate to Seaglass
White#FFFFFF · 255 255 255Canvas. Page background for every document and screen.
Slate#344C56 · 52 76 86Primary. Headings, buttons, links. 9.1:1 on white.
Seaglass#80B0A6 · 128 176 166The brand color. Panels, icon fills, section markers.
Mist#DDE6E3 · 221 230 227Soft panels, table stripes, form fields.
Charcoal Ink#22333B · 34 51 59Body text and dark surfaces. 13.1:1 on white.
Lemongrass#DBE442 · 219 228 66Accent, ≤5%.
Best for

Everything: website, PDFs, training decks, policy briefs, and family-facing materials alike — this is now the single brand system.

Watch for

Too much Slate and the Creator disappears. Seaglass must appear on every spread, not just the cover.

Palette Rules

  • Seaglass #80B0A6 is never text. At 2.4:1 on white it fails every WCAG threshold, including large text. Use it as a field, a fill, or a rule.
  • Lemongrass is capped at about five percent of any composition: a background block, an icon fill, an active state, a single highlight. It is never a page background, a heading color, or body text.
  • Slate and Charcoal Ink carry every word. All text under 24px is set in one of the two; Slate for headings, buttons, and links, Charcoal Ink for paragraphs.
  • The gradient is one transition, one direction. Slate into Seaglass. Never three-plus hues, never into Lemongrass, never behind text.
  • Keep the palette cool. No gold, orange, coral, or warm greens anywhere — Lemongrass is the only warm-adjacent note, and it stays under five percent.
  • White is the canvas. Every page and screen sits on white; Mist and Seaglass provide the panels and fields that break it up.

Contrast & Accessibility

Measured WCAG 2.1 ratios. AA requires 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text (24px+, or 19px bold) and UI components.

02

Instrument Sans & Nunito Sans

Typography · Final Pairing

The selected pairing from the exploration round. The brief asks for type that is geometric and character-driven at display size and open, tall-x-height, and legible at 14px in body — a PDF a teacher opens on her phone is the test case. Fraunces italic stays as the single warm accent, once per page at most. All three are free Google Fonts. The wordmark's "10" numeral is a drawn glyph and is not set in any of these faces.

01Pairing

Instrument Sans + Nunito Sans · Fraunces accent

Selected

Instrument Sans is a quiet geometric with a slight softness in the terminals — built, but never loud. Nunito Sans is the workhorse: open apertures, a tall x-height, and a touch of roundness that keeps dense content approachable without tipping into Caregiver. Fraunces italic is the single warm moment — the motto, a pull-quote — used once per page.

Round #2 · Logo Concepts

Refinement

Fourteen second-round directions, shown at full size on white. This round narrows to the marks that carried Round #1 — the owl, the client's chosen ambassador, and the tree and leaf family — set against quieter, lighter wordmarks with the numeral picked out in Seaglass or ink. All remain drafts: colour, proportion, and lettering will be refined for whichever directions move forward.

01Barn Owl

A resting owl with a white heart-shaped face; ink wordmark, Seaglass numeral.

02Tree Ring

A circular tree-of-life badge takes the place of the "o".

03Leaf Globe

Translucent overlapping leaves form the "o".

04Sprout Ring

A thin ring holding a two-leaf sprout as the "o"; the one Lemongrass leaf is the accent.

05Hidden Owl

An owl perched inside the "o"; Seaglass lettering, ink numeral.

06Bloom

A mosaic leaf canopy replaces the "o"; Seaglass lettering, ink numeral.

07Rooted Tree

A fine-line tree, roots and all, as the "o"; Seaglass lettering, ink numeral.

08Leaf Cluster

Overlapping leaves in all four palette colors lead the wordmark.

09Leaf Canopy

A fan of leaves rises over the wordmark; centered lockup.

10Bird Tree 0

A leafy tree with birds taking flight fills the zero of the numeral.

11Leaf Burst

A crown of leaves bursts from the "j" dot; ink wordmark, Seaglass numeral.

12Rooted Tree Mark

A full rooted tree with multicolor leaves leads the wordmark as a standalone mark.

13Curling Tree

A swirling branch flourish with Lemongrass sparks beside the wordmark.

14Perched Owl

A side-profile owl with Lemongrass eyes leads the wordmark.

Round #1 · Logo Concepts

Exploration

Fourteen first-round directions, shown at equal size on white. They explore the three ideas the assessment surfaced — the open book, the growing tree, and the numeral 10 as an ownable glyph — across a range of wordmark weights. All are drafts: colour, proportion, and lettering will be refined for whichever directions move forward.

01Sunrise Book

Open book with a rising sun and Lemongrass rays; tracked light wordmark, bold numeral.

02Ring & Pages

A circle enclosing turning pages in Lemongrass and gold; serif wordmark.

03Growth Tree

Curled branches growing out of an open book, sparks of Lemongrass; Seaglass numeral.

04Sprout Book

Outlined book with a two-leaf sprout in Lemongrass and Seaglass; Seaglass numeral.

05Leafed Tree Book

Full leafy tree rising from an open book with gold and Lemongrass pages; Seaglass numeral.

06Canopy

A Seaglass tree standing over the numeral; the wordmark sits beneath the canopy.

07Petal Book

Angled petal-page shapes in Lemongrass, gold, and ink; Seaglass numeral.

08Spark in the O

The "o" becomes a bowl of sparks in gold and ink; bold numeral.

09Graduate

A figure in a cap rising from an open book with Lemongrass wings; serif wordmark.

10Page-fold P

Stacked pages form the capital P; heavy wordmark, light Seaglass numeral.

11Folded 10

A cut-paper numeral in Lemongrass and gold; heavy wordmark.

12Ring 10

The zero as a segmented ring in every palette color; heavy wordmark.

13Overlapping 10

The 1 overlaps a Lemongrass zero; light tracked wordmark.

14Book in the 0

Turning pages set inside the zero; heavy wordmark.
